usage: Polite; handing over your receipt at the counter
반말, to a friend helping you return something
Formal 합쇼체, stiffer or to a manager
Saying you have it before you hand it over
examples: 영수증 여기 있어요.
Here's the receipt.
Said as you place the receipt on the counter
환불하려고요. 영수증 여기 있어요.
I'd like a refund. Here's the receipt.
State your purpose first, then offer the proof
어제 산 건데, 영수증 여기 있어요.
I bought it yesterday — here's the receipt.
어제 산 거 ('the thing bought yesterday') sets up the return
nuance: 영수증 여기 있어요 is 영수증 ('receipt', Sino-Korean 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it is here / here it is'), the line you say while handing your receipt to staff for a return or exchange. 여기 있어요 is the natural Korean for 'here you go / here it is' when presenting an object — it literally says 'it exists here', and the offering meaning is understood from the gesture. Keep the receipt, because almost every Korean store requires 영수증 for a refund or exchange; without it you may only get store credit or be refused. The dividing line from 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you') is formality and warmth: 영수증 드릴게요 actively announces you're giving it and is a touch more deferential, while 여기 있어요 simply presents it — both are fine, 여기 있어요 is the everyday default. The English-speaker trap is translating 'here you go' word-for-word as 여기 가요 ('here I go / I'm going here'), which is nonsense in this context; the set phrase is 여기 있어요. Another pitfall is confusing 영수증 (receipt, proof of payment) with 계산서 (the bill/itemized statement) — for a return you need the 영수증.

english: Can I get a refund on this?
usage: Can I get a refund on this?
Polite-neutral; asking if a refund is possible
반말, to a friendly small-shop owner
Is a refund possible for this?
가능하다 ('to be possible'), a common interchangeable form
examples: 이거 환불돼요?
Can I get a refund on this?
Holding up the item, asking before anything else
영수증 있는데, 이거 환불돼요?
I have the receipt — can I get a refund on this?
Lead with 영수증 있는데 to show you're prepared
한 번도 안 썼는데 이거 환불돼요?
I haven't used it once — can I get a refund?
한 번도 안 썼다 ('never used it') strengthens the case
nuance: 이거 환불돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불 ('refund', Sino-Korean 還拂) + 되다 ('to be done/possible') in polite question form — 'is a refund possible for this?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility, which is exactly right as your opening move: you ask IF a refund is possible before you ask them to actually do it. Once they say yes, you switch to the request 환불해 주세요 ('please refund it'). The dividing line is crucial: 환불돼요? asks whether it CAN be done, while 환불해 주세요 ASKS them to do it — don't merge them into one demand. Also distinguish 환불 (money back) from 교환 (exchange for another item) and 반품 (returning the goods, the physical act); 환불 specifically means getting your money back. The English-speaker error is over-translating 'can I' as a permission/ability question with 제가 …할 수 있어요?, e.g. 제가 환불할 수 있어요? — that sounds like asking about YOUR ability to issue a refund; the idiomatic ask uses the passive 되다: 환불돼요?. Another trap is the particle: don't say 이거를 환불돼요 — 되다 here is intransitive, so it's 이거 환불돼요? with no object particle.

That asks about your own ability to issue a refund and sounds backwards. Use the passive feasibility form: 이거 환불돼요? ('can this be refunded?').

usage: Polite; the standard request to be refunded
반말, to a friend or very casual seller
Could you give me a refund, please?
I'd like to request a refund
Softer, deferential with 부탁드리다 ('to request a favor')
examples: 환불해 주세요.
Please give me a refund.
Said once you've decided and shown the receipt
사이즈가 안 맞아서요. 환불해 주세요.
The size doesn't fit — please refund it.
Give the reason with -아서요, then make the request
이거 카드로 결제했는데 환불해 주세요.
I paid for this by card — please refund it.
Mention 카드로 결제 so they refund to the right method
nuance: 환불해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me', from 해 주다, the favor verb). The 해 주다 is what turns it into a courteous request for the staff's help rather than a flat command; without it (환불하세요) you'd be ordering them to refund, which sounds bossy. This is the line you use AFTER confirming a refund is possible with 환불돼요?. Note 환불 is a 하다-noun, so it needs the verb 하다: the joined form is 환불해 주세요, and you cannot say 환불 주세요 ('please give a refund') because you can't directly 'give' a refund the way you give an object. To sound extra polite — useful when staff are reluctant — soften to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요. The English-speaker error is the missing favor verb (환불하세요, too blunt) or the ungrammatical 환불 주세요. Another pitfall is register mismatch: 환불 부탁드립니다 in a casual market stall can sound oddly formal, while bare 환불 in a department store sounds rude — default to 환불해 주세요 and adjust. Also, mention your payment method (카드로 / 현금으로), since card purchases are refunded to the card by law, not in cash.

Demanding cash back for a card purchase.
By card you're refunded to the same card, not in cash (카드 결제는 카드로 환불). Say 카드로 결제했어요, 환불해 주세요, and expect the card to be credited.

usage: Polite; stating you want to swap the item
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Asking first whether an exchange is possible
examples: 이거 교환하고 싶어요.
I'd like to exchange this.
Said while presenting the item you want to swap
색깔을 바꾸고 싶어서 교환하고 싶어요.
I want a different color, so I'd like to exchange it.
색깔을 바꾸다 ('change the color') gives the reason
사이즈가 작아서 한 치수 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
It's too small, so I'd like to exchange it for one size up.
한 치수 큰 걸로 ('for one size up') specifies the swap
nuance: 교환하고 싶어요 is 교환 ('exchange', Sino-Korean 交換) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'), 'I want to exchange (this)'. Unlike ordering food — where 'I want to' (먹고 싶어요) sounds too desire-focused — for returns and exchanges 교환하고 싶어요 is perfectly natural and polite, because you're stating your purpose to staff who'll then guide you. The dividing line from 교환돼요? is that 교환돼요? checks IF an exchange is possible, while 교환하고 싶어요 declares that you WANT one; many people open with 교환하고 싶은데요… (with the soft -ㄴ데요 ender) to invite the staff to respond. Crucially, distinguish 교환 (swap for another item, same or different) from 환불 (money back) and 반품 (sending the goods back) — 교환 means you walk out with a replacement, not a refund. The English-speaker error is confusing 교환 with 변경 ('change/alter', used for reservations, plans, settings) — you 교환 a product but 변경 a booking. Another pitfall: when you want a specific replacement, mark it with -로/-으로 ('into/for'): 큰 사이즈로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환 — forgetting the -로 makes the target unclear.

To name what you're swapping for, use -로: 큰 걸로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. Without it (큰 거 교환) the target item is unclear.
Saying 교환하고 싶어요 when you actually want money back.

english: Please swap it for a different one
usage: Please swap it for a different one
Polite; asking to exchange for another item
Swap it for a different one
반말, to a friend or casual stall
Could you swap it for a different one?
Please swap it for a different color
다른 색으로 ('for a different color') when only the color is off
examples: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Please swap this for a different one.
Said when the item itself is fine but you want another
이거 흠집 있어서 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
This has a scratch — please swap it for a different one.
흠집 있다 ('has a scratch') gives the reason
같은 걸로 새 거 있으면 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
If you have a new one of the same, please swap it.
같은 걸로 새 거 ('a new one of the same') asks for a clean replacement
nuance: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is 다른 ('different/other') + 걸로 (걸 = 거 'thing' + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please change it for me'). 바꾸다 is the native verb 'to change/swap', warmer and more everyday than the Sino-Korean 교환하다 — both work, but 바꿔 주세요 is what people most naturally say at a counter. The -로 on 다른 걸로 is essential: it marks the target you're swapping INTO ('for a different one'); drop it and 다른 거 바꿔 주세요 sounds incomplete. The dividing line from 환불해 주세요 is outcome: 바꿔 주세요 gets you a replacement item, 환불해 주세요 gets you your money — don't say 바꿔 주세요 if you actually want a refund. The English-speaker error is treating 바꾸다 like English 'change' and using it for money/reservations incorrectly, or saying 다른 거 주세요 ('give me a different one') without the exchange framing — that sounds like you're starting a fresh purchase, not swapping the one you have. Another pitfall: specify what's wrong or what you want (다른 색으로, 큰 사이즈로, 새 걸로) so staff know whether it's a defect swap or a preference swap.

Saying 다른 거 주세요 to mean 'exchange this'.
That sounds like asking for a different item as a new request, not swapping the one you hold. For an exchange, use 바꿔 주세요: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.

바꾸다 swaps one item for another; it doesn't return money. If you want a refund, say 환불해 주세요.

usage: Polite; flagging a faulty product gently
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Flat statement, a touch more direct
I think it's a defective item
examples: 이거 불량인데요.
This one's defective.
Said while showing the faulty item to staff
새로 샀는데 이거 불량인데요. 작동이 안 돼요.
I just bought it, but it's defective — it doesn't work.
작동이 안 되다 ('doesn't operate') names the problem
박스 열자마자 봤는데 이거 불량인데요.
I saw it the moment I opened the box — this is defective.
박스 열자마자 ('as soon as I opened the box') shows it wasn't your fault
nuance: 이거 불량인데요 is 이거 ('this') + 불량 ('defect/defective', Sino-Korean 不良) + 인데요 (the copula 이다 + the soft ender -ㄴ데요). 불량 means the product is faulty from the maker — a manufacturing defect — and 불량품 is the noun 'a defective item'. The -ㄴ데요 ender is the politeness engine: it raises the problem as 'here's the situation…' and invites the staff to respond, so it's far gentler than a flat 이거 불량이에요, which can sound like an accusation. The dividing line from 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) is nuance: 불량 implies it doesn't work right / is faulty in function, while 하자 is a flaw or blemish (a scratch, a crack, a defect in condition); for electronics that won't turn on, 불량 fits; for a visible blemish, 하자 있어요 is more precise. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'broken' and saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new faulty item — 고장 means it broke down (often from use/over time), whereas a product that was faulty out of the box is 불량. Another pitfall: 불량 is also slang for a 'delinquent' person (불량 학생), so context matters, but with a product it clearly means defective.

The bare statement can sound accusatory. The soft ender raises it gently: 이거 불량인데요? lets staff respond without feeling blamed.
Confusing 불량 (faulty function) with 하자 (blemish/flaw).

usage: Polite; pointing out a blemish on the product
반말, to a friend or casual seller
흠집 ('scratch') for a surface mark specifically
It seems to have a bit of a flaw
examples: 여기 하자 있어요.
There's a flaw here.
Pointing right at the blemish as you say it
여기 보세요, 하자 있어요. 박음질이 터졌어요.
Look here — there's a flaw. The stitching's come apart.
박음질이 터지다 ('the stitching burst') names the exact defect
살 때는 몰랐는데 집에서 보니까 여기 하자 있어요.
I didn't notice when buying, but at home I saw a flaw here.
집에서 보니까 ('looking at home') explains the late discovery
nuance: 여기 하자 있어요 is 여기 ('here') + 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) + 있어요 ('there is'). 하자 is the precise word for a defect in condition — a scratch, crack, tear, stain, or other blemish — as opposed to 불량, which leans toward a functional fault (it doesn't work). Pointing with 여기 ('here') as you say it makes the complaint concrete and helps staff see exactly what you mean.
